chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
title: Scott Joplin's widow's after-hours apartment and Tatum's 'Danny Boy' joke
summary: They went to Joplin's blind widow's flat where Tatum played, and he teased a traditionalist pianist with an outlandish chord in Danny Boy.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: We'd leave and have breakfast, and probably leave there, go to Scott Joplin's wife's house. I told you that I had -- that we used to go there, didn't I, previously. Any way, I'm afraid of repeating myself but --
This is the first time I really was aware of -- that Scott Joplin's widow was alive. But they had this after hours spot.

Nothing, just Scott Joplin's wife. This is all he said, John, we're going to Scott Joplin's wife. She had a nice apartment, and we'd go up here and he'd buy drinks and he would play. And she was blind. But there was a guy there, I think he's a little effeminate, that lived there and he was a bartender or something, and he played piano, and he was just a traditionalist, you know. And the pure

chords, you know, one, three, five chords. And Art would upset him so badly sometimes, so Art would tell me, 'Say, watch, John, watch what I'm going to do.' So he would start playing 'Danny Boy.' This was one of this guy's favorite tunes, and he'd start playing it and then about four bars he hit one of these outrageous chords and this guy would say, Art, you boob, you don't even know the chords. And Art would die, he would just laugh, you know. Had a tremendous sense of humor. You know, and as I said, loved sports.
